name: SSH, TFTP and FTP
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Configure and verify SSH remote access on IOS, compare TFTP and FTP, and copy configs and IOS images safely.

lesson.intro: Network engineers log in remotely and move files: IOS images in, configuration backups out. Learn to configure SSH step by step on IOS, compare TFTP and FTP, use the copy command, and know why SCP and SFTP are now preferred.
objectives: Explain why SSH replaced Telnet for remote management
Configure SSH end to end on a router or a Layer 2 switch
Verify and troubleshoot SSH with show ip ssh, show ssh and a checklist
Compare TFTP and FTP by transport, ports, authentication and modes
Use the IOS file system and copy for backups and images, preferring SCP and SFTP

sections.title: Why SSH, not Telnet
sections.key: Telnet (TCP 23) sends everything, passwords included, in clear text. SSH (TCP 22) encrypts the session and always needs a username and an RSA key.
sections.body:
You need to change a VLAN on a switch two floors away, so you connect to its management address. That remote CLI session lands on one of the device's **vty lines** (virtual terminal lines), and the protocol you use matters:

[[visual]]

SSH on IOS has two requirements Telnet does not:

- It always uses a **username** as well as a password, so you need local usernames or an AAA server.
- The device needs an **RSA key pair**, which needs a hostname and a domain name first.

Remote access of any kind also needs IP connectivity. A router needs an address on a reachable interface. A Layer 2 switch needs a management SVI (such as `interface vlan 1` with an address and `no shutdown`) plus `ip default-gateway` to answer administrators on other subnets.

[[visual 2]]

items.title: Telnet
points: Everything in **clear text**: keystrokes, username, password, output
Anyone capturing traffic on the path reads the password
A strong password does not help

items.title: SSH
points: The client checks the server's public host key, so an impostor stands out
Use version 2; version 1 has known weaknesses

messages.label: Key exchange
messages.detail: encrypted channel; client checks host key

messages.label: EXEC prompt on a vty line

sections.tip: Telnet is TCP 23 and clear text; SSH is TCP 22 and encrypted.
sections.pitfall: Assuming a strong password makes Telnet safe. The password itself crosses the network in clear text, so its strength does not matter to someone capturing packets.

check.question: Why is SSH preferred over Telnet for managing network devices?
choices: SSH encrypts the session, including the login credentials
SSH uses UDP, which is faster
SSH does not need any user authentication
SSH works without an IP address on the device
check.explanation: Telnet sends usernames, passwords and all output in clear text; SSH encrypts everything. SSH runs over TCP 22, always needs a username, and like Telnet it needs IP connectivity to the device.

sections.title: Preparing the device: hostname, domain name and RSA keys
sections.key: Set a hostname and `ip domain-name`, run `crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048`, then `ip ssh version 2`. SSHv2 needs a key of at least 768 bits.
sections.body:
IOS names the SSH key pair after the device's **fully qualified domain name (FQDN)**, hostname plus domain name, so the order matters:

[[visual]]

[[code]]

**Key size**: SSH version 2 needs **at least 768 bits**. Releases offer 360 up to 2048 or 4096 bits; below 768 leaves only SSHv1. Use **2048**.

Right after the key is generated, IOS reports SSH **1.99**: it accepts both version 1 and version 2 clients. `ip ssh version 2` locks it to v2.

No reload is needed. The key is stored separately, so `show running-config` shows no key line. Save anyway, or the hostname and domain name the key depends on vanish at the next reload.

[[visual 2]]

steps.label: Set a hostname
steps.note: IOS refuses keys while it is still Router or Switch

steps.label: Set a domain name
steps.note: otherwise IOS asks you to define one first

steps.label: Generate the key pair
steps.note: named R1.lab.local; enables the SSH server. Without modulus, IOS prompts for the size

steps.label: Allow only version 2
steps.note: refused until a key of 768 bits or more exists

visual.title: Key housekeeping
rows: Replaces the key after you confirm
Deletes the keys, which disables SSH

sections.code:
Router(config)# crypto key generate rsa
% Please define a hostname other than Router.
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# crypto key generate rsa
% Please define a domain-name first.
R1(config)# ip domain-name lab.local
R1(config)# crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
The name for the keys will be: R1.lab.local
% Generating 2048 bit RSA keys, keys will be non-exportable...
[OK] (elapsed time was 3 seconds)
%SSH-5-ENABLED: SSH 1.99 has been enabled
R1(config)# ip ssh version 2
sections.tip: Order matters: hostname, then ip domain-name, then crypto key generate rsa, then ip ssh version 2.
sections.pitfall: Generating a 512-bit key and then wondering why ip ssh version 2 fails. SSHv2 needs at least 768 bits; use 2048.

check.question: What is the minimum RSA modulus that allows SSH version 2?
choices: 512 bits
360 bits
768 bits
4096 bits
check.explanation: SSHv2 requires a key of at least 768 bits. 512 and 360 are smaller, allowing only SSHv1, and 4096 is simply a large option. In practice use 2048.

sections.title: Users and vty lines
sections.key: Create users with `username ... secret`, then on every vty line configure `login local` and `transport input ssh`, so only SSH with local usernames gets in.
sections.body:
The key makes encryption possible; the vty lines decide who may log in, and how.

**Local users**: `username admin secret Str0ng!Pass` stores a strong hash. The older `username admin password ...` stores clear text or weak, reversible encryption, so prefer `secret`. Adding `privilege 15` drops the user straight into privileged EXEC.

**vty lines**: routers usually have `line vty 0 4` (five sessions), switches `line vty 0 15` (sixteen). Configure **all** of them the same way, or an attacker uses the line you forgot.

[[visual]]

Also set an `enable secret`; otherwise a vty user below privilege 15 gets `% No password set` at `enable`. Two global commands tune the SSH server: `ip ssh time-out 60` (seconds to finish logging in, default 120) and `ip ssh authentication-retries 3` (default 3).

[[code]]

visual.title: vty line commands
rows: Check the **local username database**. Plain `login` checks the line password, which has no username, so SSH cannot use it
Allow both. `none` allows neither. Defaults vary by platform, so always set it
Log idle sessions out after 10 minutes
Only source addresses permitted by standard ACL 10 may connect

sections.code:
R1(config)# username admin secret Str0ng!Pass
R1(config)# enable secret En4ble!Pass
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 10 0
R1(config-line)# end
R1# copy running-config startup-config
sections.pitfall: Configuring login instead of login local. SSH needs a username, so with only a line password every SSH login fails even though the keys and transport are right.

activity.title: Lab: secure remote access with SSH
activity.prompt: Lock R1 down to SSH only. Set a hostname and an ip domain-name, create local user admin with a secret, generate the RSA key, then on line vty 0 4 configure login local and transport input ssh. Finish with show ip ssh and read which version it reports.

check.question: Which pair of vty commands allows only SSH and authenticates against local usernames?
choices: login and transport input all
login local and transport input ssh
password cisco and transport input ssh
login local and transport input telnet
check.explanation: login local uses the username database, which SSH needs, and transport input ssh rejects Telnet. Plain login with a line password cannot authenticate SSH users, and transport input all or telnet would still allow clear-text Telnet.

sections.title: Verifying and troubleshooting SSH
sections.key: `show ip ssh` gives the server version (2.0 means v2 only, 1.99 means both) and `show ssh` lists sessions. Troubleshoot from reachability up to keys, lines, login and ACLs.
sections.body:
Two commands show the SSH server's state:

[[visual]]

To test from another Cisco device, use the IOS client: `ssh -l admin 10.0.0.1` (a lowercase L, for login name). From a PC, any SSH client works.

When SSH fails, walk the chain in order:

[[visual 2]]

The exhibit shows a healthy result: v2 only, one administrator connected, and a switch opening a session.

[[code]]

rows: Enabled or not, and the version: **2.0** accepts only SSHv2, **1.99** accepts both. Also the authentication timeout and retries. With no RSA key: SSH disabled, create keys
Sessions connected now: version, encryption, HMAC, state and username, one line per direction

steps.label: IP reachability
steps.detail: Address, interface up, a switch's `ip default-gateway`. Ping first

steps.label: RSA key exists
steps.detail: `show ip ssh` says disabled: set hostname and domain, then generate

steps.label: Key of 768 bits or more
steps.detail: Otherwise v2 cannot be enabled: regenerate with `modulus 2048`

steps.label: vty lines allow SSH
steps.detail: `transport input telnet` or `none` rejects the connection

steps.label: Login works
steps.detail: `login` instead of `login local`, no username, or a wrong password

steps.label: Not filtered
steps.detail: An `access-class` (implicit deny) or interface ACL blocks TCP 22 from that source

steps.label: Versions and algorithms match
steps.detail: An SSHv1-only client against a v2-only server, or very old IOS ciphers

sections.code:
R1# show ip ssh
SSH Enabled - version 2.0
Authentication timeout: 120 secs; Authentication retries: 3

R1# show ssh
Connection Version Mode Encryption  Hmac           State            Username
0          2.0     IN   aes256-ctr  hmac-sha2-256  Session started  admin
0          2.0     OUT  aes256-ctr  hmac-sha2-256  Session started  admin
%No SSHv1 server connections running.

SW2# ssh -l admin 10.0.0.1
Password:
R1>
sections.pitfall: Skipping the ping. Prove IP reachability first; no SSH setting can fix a missing route or a down interface.

check.question: show ip ssh reports `SSH Enabled - version 1.99`. What does that mean?
choices: SSH is running a beta release
Only SSH version 1 is accepted
SSH is disabled until a key is generated
Both SSH version 1 and version 2 clients are accepted
check.explanation: 1.99 is how IOS reports that both versions are allowed. After ip ssh version 2 it shows 2.0. A device with no key reports SSH as disabled instead.

sections.title: SSH on a switch, end to end
sections.key: A Layer 2 switch needs a management SVI that is up/up and an ip default-gateway before SSH works from other subnets; then the router recipe applies on vty 0 15.
sections.body:
New access switch SW1 (hostname already set) must be managed from the 10.9.9.0/24 operations subnet:

[[visual]]

A Layer 2 switch has no routed interfaces, so it gets a management **SVI**. The SVI comes up only when VLAN 10 exists and at least one port in VLAN 10 (access or trunk) is up. The switch does not route, so without `ip default-gateway` it answers its own subnet but not 10.9.9.0/24.

[[visual 2]]

Defaults differ: switches typically allow `transport input all` on vty lines, many routers `none`. Set it explicitly either way.

Test with `ssh netadmin@10.1.10.5` from a PC or `ssh -l netadmin 10.1.10.5` from a Cisco device, then check `show ip ssh`, `show ssh` and `show running-config | section line vty`. On a router the same recipe applies without the SVI and default gateway.

steps.label: An address: the management SVI
steps.work:
interface vlan 10
 ip address 10.1.10.5 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown

steps.label: Identity and keys
steps.work:
ip domain-name lab.local
crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
ip ssh version 2

steps.label: Who may log in
steps.work:
username netadmin secret N3t!Admin
enable secret En4ble!Pass

steps.label: All 16 vty lines
steps.work:
line vty 0 15
 login local
 transport input ssh

steps.label: Save, or a reload strands the switch

sections.tip: Switch SSH checklist: SVI up, default gateway, hostname, domain, key, version 2, user, vty 0 15 with login local and transport input ssh, then save.
sections.pitfall: Forgetting ip default-gateway on a Layer 2 switch. SSH works from the switch's own subnet and fails everywhere else, which looks like an SSH problem but is a routing one.

check.question: How many vty lines does a typical Catalyst switch have, and which command configures them all at once?
choices: 5, with line vty 0 4
16, with line vty 0 15
4, with line vty 1 4
15, with line vty 1 15
check.explanation: Switches number their 16 vty lines 0 through 15, so line vty 0 15 covers them all. Routers commonly have 0 to 4. Leaving some lines unconfigured leaves a back door open.

sections.title: TFTP and FTP compared
sections.key: TFTP uses UDP 69 with no login and only get and put; FTP uses TCP 21 for control plus separate data connections and supports logins. Neither encrypts.
sections.body:
Engineers move files all the time: IOS images into flash, configuration backups out, configuration files down to IP phones. Two classic protocols do it:

[[visual]]

TFTP is tiny enough to live in boot code, ROMMON and IP phones. Cisco IP phones learn a TFTP server address from DHCP and download their configuration from it at boot.

FTP opens its data connections in one of two modes:

[[visual 2]]

**Neither TFTP nor FTP encrypts anything.** FTP's login crosses the network in clear text, like Telnet's. A sensible TFTP habit: run a server on a laptop for ten minutes on an isolated lab or management network, then turn it off.

rows: **TCP 21** control connection, plus TCP data connections
Its own: numbered blocks, each acknowledged before the next
Username and password, in clear text
**Get and put only**: no listing, no deleting
List, navigate, get, put, rename, delete
IOS images, phone configs, quick lab transfers

items.title: Active mode
points: The client announces a listening port with PORT
The **server** opens the data connection back to it (traditionally from TCP 20)
Firewalls and NAT in front of the client block that inbound connection

items.title: Passive mode
points: The server picks a port, tells the client and waits
The **client** opens both connections, so it works through firewalls and NAT: the usual choice

sections.tip: TFTP: UDP 69, no login, get and put only. FTP: TCP 21 plus data connections, logins, full file management.
sections.pitfall: Saying TFTP uses TCP because it is reliable. It runs over UDP 69 and builds its own minimal acknowledgment scheme on top.

check.question: Which statement correctly compares TFTP and FTP?
choices: TFTP uses TCP and supports logins; FTP uses UDP and does not
Both encrypt credentials by default
TFTP uses UDP and has no authentication; FTP uses TCP and supports usernames and passwords
TFTP supports directory listings and FTP does not
check.explanation: TFTP runs on UDP 69 with no login and only get and put. FTP runs on TCP (control on 21) with logins and full file management. Neither encrypts, which is why SCP and SFTP exist.

sections.title: The IOS file system
sections.key: IOS names storage with prefixes: flash: holds images, nvram: the startup-config, system: the running-config in RAM, and tftp:, ftp: and scp: are remote servers.
sections.body:
Every copy command names locations in the **IOS File System (IFS)**. `show file systems` lists them, each with a **prefix** ending in a colon; the asterisk marks the default:

[[visual]]

Everyday commands use these names:

[[visual 2]]

A full URL such as `tftp://10.0.0.5/r1-confg` or `ftp://user:pass@10.0.0.5/image.bin` saves copy from asking questions. Always check free space before copying an image:

[[code]]

[[visual 3]]

rows: IOS images and saved files; survives reloads
Internal files, including the **running-config** in RAM
Remote servers reached with that protocol
A USB drive in the router
The default flash; ends with bytes available and used
Any file system's files; ends with bytes total and free

visual.title: flash0: on R2 (256 MB)
visual.caption: It will not fit until an old image goes: `delete flash0:c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.152-4.M1.bin`.

sections.code:
R2# show file systems
File Systems:

           -           -    opaque     rw   system:
           -           -   network     rw   tftp:
*  256487424    49238016      disk     rw   flash0: flash:#
      262136      253220     nvram     rw   nvram:
           -           -   network     rw   ftp:
  7794737152  7483719680  usbflash     rw   usbflash0:

R2# dir flash0:
Directory of flash0:/
    1  -rw-  104193476  Jul 21 2015 13:38:06 +00:00  c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.154-3.M3.bin
    9  -rw-   97794040  Oct 10 2014 21:06:38 +00:00  c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.152-4.M1.bin
256487424 bytes total (49238016 bytes free)
sections.tip: Prefixes end in a colon: flash:, nvram:, system:, tftp:. Running-config is in system:, startup-config in nvram:.
sections.pitfall: Assuming the running-config lives in NVRAM. It is in RAM (system:running-config) and vanishes at reload; NVRAM holds the startup-config.

check.question: Which file system holds the startup-config by default?
choices: flash:
system:
nvram:
tftp:
check.explanation: The startup-config is nvram:startup-config. flash: holds IOS images, system: holds the running-config in RAM, and tftp: is a remote server.

sections.title: Copying files: backups and IOS images
sections.key: `copy` is always source then destination: running-config startup-config saves, running-config tftp: backs up, tftp: running-config merges, and tftp: flash: loads an image.
sections.body:
On IOS the `copy` command moves files, always as **copy source destination**. The running-config in RAM is what the device does now; the startup-config in NVRAM is what it loads at boot.

[[visual]]

The classic IOS upgrade:

[[visual 2]]

In every case the router is the **client**: it connects to the TFTP or FTP server, which can be an app on a laptop, a Linux machine or a central file server.

[[code]]

rows: Saves your changes (`write memory` is the older form). Forget it and they vanish at reload
Backs up; prompts for the server and offers a file name such as `r1-confg`
Restores by **merging** the file into the running configuration, not replacing it
Loads an IOS image into flash
FTP with credentials in the URL, or set `ip ftp username` and `ip ftp password` once. Clear text either way

steps.label: Copy the image in
steps.detail: `copy tftp: flash:`, answering the prompts. Press Enter to accept a default name: typing y names the file y

steps.label: Check it against Cisco's published hash
Point the boot at it and save

sections.code:
R1# copy running-config tftp:
Address or name of remote host []? 10.0.0.5
Destination filename [r1-confg]?
!!
1384 bytes copied in 0.512 secs (2703 bytes/sec)

R1# copy tftp: flash:
Address or name of remote host []? 10.0.0.5
Source filename []? c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.155-3.M.bin
Destination filename [c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.155-3.M.bin]?
Accessing tftp://10.0.0.5/c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.155-3.M.bin...
[OK - 107410736 bytes]
107410736 bytes copied in 211.302 secs (508330 bytes/sec)
sections.pitfall: Reading copy backwards. Source comes first: copy running-config tftp: backs up, while copy tftp: running-config restores by merging.

check.question: Which command backs up the router's current configuration to a TFTP server?
choices: copy running-config tftp:
copy tftp: running-config
copy startup-config running-config
copy flash: tftp: running-config
check.explanation: copy takes the source first and the destination second, so running-config to tftp: is the backup. copy tftp: running-config is the restore, which merges, and copying startup to running loads the saved configuration.

sections.title: Secure alternatives: SCP and SFTP
sections.key: SCP and SFTP move files over SSH on TCP 22, encrypting the login and the contents; FTPS is FTP with TLS. Prefer them to TFTP and FTP.
sections.body:
Configuration files hold password hashes, SNMP communities and VPN keys, and images must be trustworthy. Move them over SSH instead of in clear text:

[[visual]]

- **SCP** works with the same copy command, as in the example below. A router or switch can also be an SCP server (`ip scp server enable`, which also needs AAA authorization), so you can push an image from a laptop.
- **SFTP** adds FTP-like listing and navigation. Despite the name, it is a separate protocol built on SSH, not FTP with security added. That is **FTPS**.

[[visual 2]]

Still run `verify` on an image: encryption protects the transfer, not the file's origin. TFTP keeps a niche where devices speak nothing else (ROMMON recovery, IP phones); keep those servers on protected networks.

[[code]]

visual.title: What SSH adds
rows: Credentials and file contents cannot be read in transit
Users log in, and the client checks the server's host key
visual.caption: It reuses the SSH keys and users you already set up for remote access.

sections.code:
R1# copy scp://admin@10.0.0.5/r1-backup.cfg flash:
Destination filename [r1-backup.cfg]?
Password:
!
2048 bytes copied in 1.204 secs (1701 bytes/sec)
sections.pitfall: Thinking SFTP is FTP plus encryption. SFTP is a different protocol that runs over SSH on TCP 22; FTP over TLS is called FTPS.

check.question: An engineer must copy a configuration backup across an untrusted network. Which option protects both the login and the file contents?
choices: TFTP
SCP
FTP in passive mode
FTP with ip ftp password configured
check.explanation: SCP runs over SSH, so the login and the file are encrypted. TFTP has no login and no encryption, and FTP sends its password and data in clear text whatever mode it uses or wherever the password is stored.

keyTerms.definition: A virtual terminal line that receives remote CLI sessions; routers usually have vty 0 4 and switches vty 0 15.
Remote CLI protocol on TCP 23 that sends everything, including passwords, in clear text.
Secure Shell: encrypted remote CLI on TCP 22 that needs RSA keys and usernames. Use version 2.
Created with crypto key generate rsa and named after the FQDN; at least 768 bits for SSHv2, 2048 recommended.
Fully qualified domain name: hostname plus domain name, such as R1.lab.local.
vty line command that authenticates users against the local username database.
vty line command that allows only SSH and rejects Telnet.
Shows whether SSH is enabled and the version: 2.0 for v2 only, 1.99 for both.
Trivial File Transfer Protocol: UDP 69, no authentication, get and put only.
File Transfer Protocol: TCP control connection on port 21 plus data connections; usernames and passwords in clear text.
Secure Copy Protocol: copies files over SSH on TCP 22, encrypted and authenticated.
SSH File Transfer Protocol: a separate protocol over SSH on TCP 22, not FTP with encryption (that is FTPS).
How IOS names storage: prefixes such as flash:, nvram:, system:, tftp: and usbflash0:, shown by show file systems.
The active configuration in RAM (system:running-config) and the saved one in NVRAM (nvram:startup-config) loaded at boot.
The router a Layer 2 switch sends management replies to for other subnets; without it, remote SSH to the switch fails.
Active: the server opens the data connection back to the client. Passive: the client opens it to a port the server announced, which works through firewalls and NAT.

summary: Telnet (TCP 23) is clear text; SSH (TCP 22) encrypts and always needs a username.
SSH: hostname, ip domain-name, crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048, ip ssh version 2, username secret, login local, transport input ssh.
A Layer 2 switch also needs an up/up SVI and ip default-gateway.
TFTP: UDP 69, no login, get and put. FTP: TCP 21 plus data connections, logins, passive mode through firewalls. Neither encrypts.
flash: holds images, nvram: the startup-config, system: the running-config; copy is always source, then destination.
SCP and SFTP over SSH (TCP 22) are the secure choices; still verify /md5 before booting an image.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a new colleague why the team bans Telnet and plain TFTP, walk through everything a Cisco router needs before it accepts an SSH login, and describe how you would back up its configuration safely.

questions.question: Which transport and port does SSH use?
choices: TCP 23
TCP 22
UDP 22
TCP 21
questions.explanation: SSH uses TCP 22. TCP 23 is Telnet and TCP 21 is the FTP control connection.

questions.question: What is the main security problem with Telnet?
choices: It sends everything, including passwords, in clear text
It cannot authenticate users at all
It works only on the console line
It uses UDP, so sessions drop easily
questions.explanation: Telnet does support passwords and runs over TCP 23, but nothing is encrypted, so anyone capturing the traffic can read the credentials and the session.

questions.question: Which two settings must exist before `crypto key generate rsa` succeeds? (Choose two.)
choices: A hostname other than the default
An IP domain name
A local username
transport input ssh on the vty lines
An enable secret
questions.explanation: The key is named after the FQDN, hostname plus domain name, so both must be set. Usernames and vty settings are needed to log in, but not to generate the key.

questions.question: Type the global command that generates a 2048-bit RSA key pair for SSH without being prompted for the size.
accept: crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 2048
questions.explanation: crypto key generate rsa creates the key pair named after the hostname and domain name. The modulus keyword sets the size; SSHv2 needs at least 768 bits.

questions.question: Type the global command that restricts the SSH server to version 2.
questions.explanation: By default IOS accepts versions 1 and 2 (shown as 1.99). ip ssh version 2 accepts only SSHv2, which needs an RSA key of at least 768 bits.

questions.question: Type the global command that sets the domain name lab.local, which IOS needs before it will generate RSA keys.
questions.explanation: The domain name and hostname form the FQDN used to name the key, for example R1.lab.local. Newer releases also accept the form ip domain name.

questions.question: What must the administrator do next?
questions.code:
Router(config)# crypto key generate rsa
% Please define a hostname other than Router.
choices: Add the modulus keyword to the command
Configure transport input ssh first
Configure a hostname other than Router
Enter the command in privileged EXEC mode
questions.explanation: IOS will not generate a key while the hostname is the default, because the key is named after the hostname and domain name. Set a hostname (and a domain name) first.

questions.question: An engineer generated a 512-bit RSA key. What happens when `ip ssh version 2` is entered?
choices: SSHv2 is enabled with weaker encryption
The key is regenerated automatically at 2048 bits
SSH is disabled until the device reloads
IOS refuses, because SSHv2 needs a key of at least 768 bits
questions.explanation: SSHv2 requires at least a 768-bit key, so IOS rejects the command and SSH stays at version 1 only. Regenerate the key with modulus 2048 and enter the command again.

questions.question: A router has hostname R1 and domain name lab.local. What name does IOS give its RSA key pair?
choices: R1.lab.local
lab.local.R1
R1
rsa-key-1
questions.explanation: IOS names the key after the FQDN, hostname then domain name, and prints it as it generates the key: The name for the keys will be: R1.lab.local.

questions.question: You are in line configuration mode for vty 0 4. Type the command that permits only SSH connections.
questions.explanation: transport input ssh allows SSH and rejects Telnet on these lines. transport input telnet ssh or all would allow both.

questions.question: In vty line configuration mode, type the command that makes the lines authenticate against the local username database.
questions.explanation: login local checks usernames and passwords configured with the username command. Plain login uses only the line password, which SSH cannot use.

questions.question: Type the global command that creates user admin with the hashed password Str0ng!Pass.
questions.explanation: username ... secret stores a strong hash of the password. The password keyword stores it in clear text or with weak encryption, so secret is preferred.

questions.question: Administrators can reach R1 on TCP 22, but every SSH login fails. Based on the exhibit, what is the fix?
questions.code:
R1# show ip ssh
SSH Enabled - version 2.0
Authentication timeout: 120 secs; Authentication retries: 3

R1# show running-config | section username|line vty
username admin secret 5 $1$mERr$hx5rVt7rPNoS4wqbXKX7m0
line vty 0 4
 password Cisco123
 login
 transport input ssh
choices: Add transport input telnet to the vty lines
Replace login with login local on the vty lines
Regenerate the RSA key with a 4096-bit modulus
Change ip ssh version 2 back to version 1
questions.explanation: SSH is enabled at version 2 and the lines accept SSH, but plain login checks the line password, which has no username, so SSH authentication fails. login local makes the lines use the admin account that already exists.

questions.question: Based on the exhibit from a switch, what is the risk?
questions.code:
SW1# show running-config | section line vty
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
line vty 5 15
 password Cisco123
 login
 transport input telnet
choices: SSH stops working on every line
The switch rejects all remote connections
Telnet logins with clear-text passwords are still possible on lines 5 to 15
There is no risk, because only lines 0 to 4 are ever used
questions.explanation: When lines 0 to 4 are busy, or an attacker opens several sessions, new connections land on lines 5 to 15, which accept Telnet with a shared clear-text password. Configure every vty line the same way.

questions.question: The vty lines already have login local and transport input ssh. Based on the exhibit, what is the most likely cause?
questions.code:
R1# show ip ssh
SSH Disabled - version 1.99
%Please create RSA keys to enable SSH (and of atleast 768 bits for SSH v2).
choices: The username lacks privilege 15
The exec-timeout is too short
ip ssh version 2 is configured
No RSA key pair has been generated
questions.explanation: The SSH server only runs once an RSA key exists. Generate it (after setting the hostname and domain name). Privilege levels and timeouts affect sessions, not whether the server runs.

questions.question: Which command lists the SSH sessions currently connected to a router, with their encryption and usernames?
choices: show ssh
show ip ssh
show crypto key mypubkey rsa
show line ssh
questions.explanation: show ssh lists active SSH connections. show ip ssh shows the server's version and settings, and show crypto key mypubkey rsa displays the public key.

questions.question: From another Cisco device, type the command that opens an SSH session to 10.0.0.1 as user admin.
questions.explanation: The IOS SSH client uses -l (a lowercase L) for the login name, followed by the destination address or name.

questions.question: An administrator at 10.5.5.20 cannot SSH to R1, but one at 10.1.1.20 can. R1's vty lines have `access-class 10 in`, and the only ACL entry is `access-list 10 permit 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255`. Why?
choices: access-class applies only to Telnet
ACL 10 permits only 10.1.1.0/24, and its implicit deny blocks 10.5.5.20
The RSA key only allows one subnet
SSH requires both administrators to be on the same subnet
questions.explanation: access-class filters which source addresses may open vty sessions, for SSH and Telnet alike. Every ACL ends with an implicit deny, so 10.5.5.20 is refused. Add a permit for the second administrator's address or subnet.

questions.question: Put the events in order, from an administrator starting an SSH connection to getting a prompt.
items: Client and server agree on the SSH version and algorithms
Key exchange builds the encrypted channel and the client checks the server's host key
The username and password are checked, here against the local database
The administrator gets an EXEC prompt on a vty line
questions.explanation: SSH runs over TCP, so the TCP connection comes first. The encrypted channel is built before any credentials are sent, which is exactly why the password is safe, and only then is the user authenticated.

questions.question: Which transport and port does TFTP use?
choices: TCP 69
TCP 21
UDP 69
UDP 20
questions.explanation: TFTP runs on UDP 69 and adds its own block-by-block acknowledgments. TCP 21 is the FTP control connection.

questions.question: Match each protocol to its transport and port.
questions.explanation: Only SCP (and SFTP) on TCP 22 and FTPS on 990 or 21 encrypt anything. TFTP, FTP and Telnet are all clear text.

questions.question: Which three statements about TFTP are true? (Choose three.)
choices: It uses UDP port 69
It has no user authentication
It can only get and put files, with no directory listing
It encrypts file contents
It uses a separate control connection on TCP 21
questions.explanation: TFTP is UDP 69, with no login and only get and put. It encrypts nothing, and the control connection on TCP 21 belongs to FTP.

questions.question: Why does FTP active mode often fail when the client sits behind a firewall or NAT?
choices: Active mode uses UDP, which firewalls drop
Active mode requires TFTP on port 69
The control connection cannot cross NAT
The server opens the data connection back to the client, and the firewall blocks it
questions.explanation: In active mode the server initiates each data connection toward the client, an unsolicited inbound connection that firewalls and NAT normally block. Passive mode has the client open the data connection instead.

questions.question: Which FTP connection carries commands such as the login and directory changes?
choices: The data connection, from TCP port 20
The control connection, to TCP port 21
A UDP exchange on port 69
An SSH channel on TCP 22
questions.explanation: FTP uses a control connection to port 21 for commands and replies, and separate data connections for file contents and listings.

questions.question: What does `copy tftp: running-config` do?
choices: Merges the commands in the file into the running configuration
Replaces the running configuration exactly with the file
Backs up the running configuration to the TFTP server
Saves the file to NVRAM as the startup configuration
questions.explanation: Copying into the running configuration applies the file's commands on top of what is already there, so settings missing from the file stay in place. The source comes first, so this is a restore, not a backup.

questions.question: Type the command that copies the running configuration to a TFTP server. IOS will prompt for the server and file name.
questions.explanation: copy always takes the source first and the destination second. IOS then prompts for the server address and offers a default file name such as r1-confg.

questions.question: Type the command that copies an IOS image from a TFTP server into flash. IOS will prompt for the details.
questions.explanation: The source is the TFTP server and the destination is flash. IOS prompts for the server, the source file name and the destination name.

questions.question: Which statement about the command in the exhibit is true?
choices: R1 acts as an FTP server for 10.0.0.5
The transfer is encrypted because the credentials are in the URL
R1 acts as an FTP client, and the credentials cross the network unencrypted
The file is copied from R1's flash to the server
questions.explanation: The router is the FTP client pulling the image from 10.0.0.5 into flash (source first, destination second). FTP sends the username and password in clear text no matter how they are supplied.

questions.question: After copying a new IOS image into flash, which command checks it against Cisco's published hash?
choices: show flash: hash
boot system flash:filename
copy flash: verify
verify /md5 flash:filename
questions.explanation: verify /md5 calculates the file's MD5 hash so you can compare it with the value Cisco publishes. boot system only tells the router which image to load next time.

questions.question: Put the steps of an IOS upgrade from a TFTP server in order.
items: Check free space with show flash:
Copy the image in with copy tftp: flash:
Configure boot system flash:filename and save the configuration
questions.explanation: Make room first, copy the image, prove it is intact and genuine, point the boot process at it and save, then reload into the new image.

questions.question: Which file transfer method encrypts the transfer by running over SSH?
choices: TFTP
SCP
FTP
FTP in active mode
questions.explanation: SCP uses an SSH session on TCP 22, so the login and the file are encrypted. TFTP and FTP send everything in clear text.

questions.question: What is SFTP?
choices: A file transfer protocol that runs over SSH on TCP 22
FTP with TLS encryption added
A secure version of TFTP on UDP 69
FTP limited to one file per session
questions.explanation: SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol, a separate protocol carried inside SSH. FTP with TLS is called FTPS, and there is no secure TFTP on UDP 69.

questions.question: A company bans clear-text management protocols. Which pair should replace Telnet and TFTP?
choices: SNMPv2c and FTP
HTTPS and FTP
SSH and FTP in passive mode
SSH and SCP
questions.explanation: SSH replaces Telnet for the CLI, and SCP (or SFTP) replaces TFTP for files, both encrypted over TCP 22. FTP in any mode and SNMPv2c are still clear text.

questions.question: Compare TFTP and FTP.
questions.answer: TFTP uses UDP 69, has no authentication and can only get and put files; it is tiny and common for IOS images and boot files. FTP uses TCP (control on port 21 plus data connections), supports usernames and passwords and full file management. Neither encrypts.
questions.explanation: For anything sensitive, use SCP or SFTP over SSH instead.

questions.question: Which file does `show running-config` display?
choices: nvram:running-config, saved in NVRAM
system:running-config, held in RAM
flash:running-config, stored with the IOS image
tftp:running-config, fetched from a server
questions.explanation: show running-config is a shortcut for system:running-config, the active configuration in RAM, which is lost at reload. The saved copy is nvram:startup-config, and flash holds IOS images.

questions.question: Based on the exhibit, can a 107,410,736-byte IOS image be copied into flash0: without deleting anything?
questions.code:
R2# dir flash0:
Directory of flash0:/
    1  -rw-  104193476  Jul 21 2015 13:38:06 +00:00  c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.154-3.M3.bin
    9  -rw-   97794040  Oct 10 2014 21:06:38 +00:00  c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.152-4.M1.bin
256487424 bytes total (49238016 bytes free)
choices: No; only 49,238,016 bytes are free
Yes; flash0: holds 256,487,424 bytes
Yes; copy compresses the image as it writes it
No; flash0: can store only one IOS image
questions.explanation: dir reports total capacity and free space. Two images already use most of the 256 MB, leaving about 49 MB, less than half of what the new image needs. Delete an old image first. Flash can hold several images, and copy does not compress.

questions.question: Match each IOS file system prefix to what it holds.

pairs.right: IOS images and other files kept across reloads
A TFTP server reached over the network
A USB drive plugged into the router

questions.explanation: show file systems lists every prefix with its type: disk for flash, nvram for NVRAM, opaque for logical ones such as system:, network for servers, and usbflash for USB drives.

questions.question: Type the command that lists the files in the router's flash file system.
questions.explanation: dir works on any file system and ends with bytes total and bytes free. show flash lists the default flash file system and ends with bytes available and bytes used.

questions.question: Type the command that saves the running configuration so it survives a reload.
questions.explanation: Copying the running-config to the startup-config writes it to NVRAM, which the router loads at boot. write memory does the same job on most IOS releases.

questions.question: Type the global command that makes the router boot c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.155-3.M.bin from flash at the next reload.
questions.explanation: boot system tells IOS which image to load. Save the configuration before reloading, or the router falls back to its old boot behavior.

questions.question: Admins in VLAN 10 can SSH to SW1, but admins on 10.9.9.0/24 cannot. show ip ssh reports SSH Enabled - version 2.0. Based on the configuration, what is wrong?
questions.code:
! SW1 configuration (excerpt)
hostname SW1
ip domain-name lab.local
ip ssh version 2
username netadmin secret N3t!Admin
access-list 10 permit 10.9.9.0 0.0.0.255
!
interface Vlan10
 ip address 10.1.10.5 255.255.255.0
!
line vty 0 15
 access-class 10 in
 login local
 transport input ssh
choices: access-list 10 blocks 10.9.9.0/24
transport input ssh allows only the local subnet
SW1 has no ip default-gateway, so it cannot send replies to other subnets
The RSA key must be generated separately for each subnet
questions.explanation: A Layer 2 switch does not route, so replies to any off-subnet address need ip default-gateway. Without it, SSH works only from VLAN 10. The ACL permits 10.9.9.0/24, transport input has nothing to do with subnets, and one key serves every client.

questions.question: In FTP active mode, which device opens the data connection?
choices: The client, to a port the server announced after PASV
Neither; data travels over the control connection on port 21
The client, always to server port 69
The server, connecting back to a port the client announced with PORT
questions.explanation: In active mode the server initiates the data connection toward the client, which is why firewalls and NAT in front of the client often block it. Passive mode reverses that: the client sends PASV and opens the data connection itself. Port 69 is TFTP.

questions.question: Which statement about Cisco IP phones and TFTP is true?
choices: Phones learn a TFTP server address from DHCP and download their configuration files from it
Phones use TFTP to carry voice packets during a call
Phones need FTP usernames from DHCP before TFTP works
Phones use TFTP because it encrypts their configuration files
questions.explanation: DHCP can hand out a TFTP server address along with the usual settings, and IP phones fetch their configuration files from it at boot. Voice travels in RTP over UDP, TFTP has no usernames, and it encrypts nothing.

questions.question: A Layer 2 switch must accept SSH from administrators on another subnet. Which three of these are required? (Choose three.)
choices: An IP address on a management SVI that is up/up
ip default-gateway pointing at a router on that SVI's subnet
An RSA key generated after the hostname and domain name are set
ip routing enabled globally
ip helper-address on the management SVI
questions.explanation: The SVI gives the switch an address, the default gateway lets it answer other subnets, and the RSA key enables the SSH server. ip routing would turn it into a Layer 3 switch, which is not needed, and ip helper-address relays DHCP. Usernames and vty settings are also required, but they are not among the choices.
